title: should / ought to / needn't — Advice and Absence of Obligation
grammarTitle: should / ought to / needn't — Advice and Absence of Obligation
grammarNote: "Should" и "ought to" используются для выражения СОВЕТА или РЕКОМЕНДАЦИИ — когда что-то является хорошей идеей, но не строгим обязательством. "Needn't" (= "don't need to") выражает ОТСУТСТВИЕ необходимости — как и "don't have to". Все эти глаголы выражают более мягкие степени обязательства по сравнению с "must".

grammarTable.subject: should
grammarTable.example: "You should read your email daily." / "She should see a doctor."

grammarTable.subject: shouldn't
grammarTable.example: "You shouldn't skip lectures." / "He shouldn't wait too long."

grammarTable.subject: ought to
grammarTable.example: "You ought to contact your supervisor." / "We ought to leave now."

grammarTable.subject: needn't
grammarTable.example: "You needn't arrive early — the doors open at 8." / "She needn't worry."

grammarTable.subject: need to
grammarTable.example: "You need to check the handbook." (= you must / it's important)

grammarTable.subject: Should I?
grammarTable.example: "Should I apply for the internship?" / "Should we bring a dictionary?"

grammarExtra.title: should vs ought to — the difference

rows.form: Both mean: it's a good idea / recommended
rows.example: "You should contact her." ≈ "You ought to contact her."

rows.form: "should" is more common in spoken English
rows.example: "Should I email her?" / "You should check the rules."

rows.form: "ought to" sounds more formal or emphatic
rows.example: "You really ought to speak to your adviser this week."
"You shouldn't skip the briefing." (oughtn't to = very rare, avoid it)

grammarExtra.title: needn't vs don't have to — similar meaning

rows.form: Both mean: no obligation, not necessary
rows.example: "You needn't come early." = "You don't have to come early." ✅
"Needn't" is common in British English. "Don't have to" is more universal.
"You needn't BRING your laptop." (NOT "needn't to bring")
"You need to check your email." = "You have to check your email."

grammarExtra.title: The obligation scale — from strong to weak

rows.example: "You must attend 80%." — OBLIGATORY. Not doing it has serious consequences.
"You should check your email." — RECOMMENDED. Not doing it may cause problems.
"You don't have to buy the book." — OPTIONAL. No consequences either way.
"You mustn't plagiarise." — PROHIBITED. Doing it has serious consequences.
"You should speak to your adviser." (direct advice)
"You shouldn't wait until the last minute." (negative advice)
"I think you should apply for the internship." (softened advice)

rows.form: Maybe you should / Perhaps you should
rows.example: "Maybe you should take a day off." (gentle suggestion)
"Should I email Professor Sultanova first?" (seeking recommendation)

grammarTip:
"Should" и "ought to" — совет. "Needn't" — отсутствие необходимости:
① should / ought to = хорошая идея, рекомендация → "You should read your email daily."
② shouldn't = плохая идея → "You shouldn't wait too long."
③ needn't = не нужно, не обязательно → "You needn't worry." = "You don't have to worry."

💡 Шкала обязательности:
must/have to > should/ought to > needn't/don't have to
mustn't = совсем другое — это ЗАПРЕТ!

⚠️ "Should" НЕ ИЗМЕНЯЕТСЯ по лицам:
✅ "She should check her email." (NOT "she shoulds"!)

exercises.text: Kamila is tired and her grades are falling. "___ take a break this weekend."
exercises.hint: "should" = advice/recommendation. "She SHOULD take a break." Not compulsory but a good idea. ✅

exercises.text: "You ___ (not / wait) until the last minute to apply."
exercises.hint: Negative advice → "shouldn't". "You SHOULDN'T wait until the last minute." ✅

exercises.text: "You ___ memorise every rule — the handbook is online and can be checked anytime."
exercises.hint: "needn't" = no necessity; it's not required. The handbook is available. ✅

exercises.text: "Ought to" is always more polite than "should" and should be used instead.
exercises.hint: "should" is more common in spoken English. "ought to" is slightly more formal but NOT always more polite. Use "should" for most situations.

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct form to ask for advice.
exercises.text: "___ I contact Professor Sultanova before applying?"
exercises.hint: "Should I...?" = asking for advice or recommendation. "SHOULD I contact her?" ✅

exercises.text: "You ___ (ought to / speak) to your academic adviser at least once per semester."
exercises.hint: "ought to" + base verb. "You OUGHT TO SPEAK to your adviser." ✅ (similar to "should")

exercises.text: "I think you ___ apply for the internship — it's a great opportunity."
exercises.hint: "I think you should..." = softened personal recommendation. Not a command, just a suggestion. ✅

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct modal for the scale.
exercises.text: "Which is stronger obligation: should or must?"
exercises.hint: Scale: must > should > needn't. "Must" = strong obligation. "Should" = recommendation.

exercises.text: "You don't have to worry — everything is arranged." → "You ___ worry."
exercises.hint: "needn't" = "don't have to". "You NEEDN'T worry." ✅ (both mean no necessity)

exercises.text: "She ___ (should / check) her email more carefully — she missed an important deadline."
exercises.hint: "should" + BASE VERB (no -s, no "to", no -ing!). "She SHOULD CHECK her email." ✅

exercises.text: "Maybe you should take the optional workshop." — What does this express?
exercises.hint: "Maybe you should" = very gentle, non-threatening advice. The softest way to suggest something.

questions.hint: "should" = advice/recommendation. "You SHOULD read your email." — good idea, not compulsory. ✅

questions.text: "You ___ worry — the deadline is next week." (no need)
questions.hint: "needn't" = no necessity. "You NEEDN'T worry." = It's not necessary to worry. ✅

questions.text: "She ___ skip lectures — it will affect her grade." (negative advice)
questions.hint: "shouldn't" = negative advice. "She SHOULDN'T skip lectures." — bad idea. ✅
"ought to" = formal recommendation. "You OUGHT TO contact supervisors soon." ≈ "You should." ✅

questions.text: "She shoulds check her email" is correct.
questions.hint: ✅ "She SHOULD check her email." — "should" NEVER adds -s! Same form for all subjects.

questions.text: "___ I bring a dictionary to the exam?" (asking for advice)
questions.hint: "Should I...?" = asking for advice/recommendation. "SHOULD I bring a dictionary?" ✅

questions.text: "You ___ (needn't / arrive) before 9 — the building opens then."

questions.hint: Scale: must > should/ought to > needn't. "Must" = strongest. "Should/ought to" = moderate. "Needn't" = no obligation.
"needn't" ≈ "don't have to" — both express no obligation, no necessity.

questions.text: "I think you ___ (should / apply) — it's a great opportunity."
questions.hint: "I think you should..." = softened recommendation. "I think you SHOULD APPLY." ✅
✅ "Should" NEVER changes. "She should. He should. They should." Always the same form.

questions.text: "Maybe you should take a break." — This is:
questions.hint: "Maybe you should" = a very soft, non-threatening recommendation. The gentlest advice form.
"shouldn't" = negative advice = "it's not a good idea to..." ✅
"ought to" + base verb. "You OUGHT TO THINK carefully." ✅

questions.text: "You needn't attend the optional session." — What does this mean?
opts: You are strongly advised to attend
questions.hint: "needn't" = no necessity. "You needn't attend" = it's optional. NOT forbidden.

questions.text: "Should" vs "must": which is more appropriate for personal advice?
questions.hint: "should" = personal advice/recommendation. "must" = strong obligation. For advice to a friend: "You should see a doctor." Not "You must see a doctor." (too strong).
